passages.title: The Myth of the Mindless Mob
passages.passage:
A. For more than a century the received wisdom about crowds ran roughly as follows: put enough people together, take away their names, and something ancient rises to the surface. Individuals who would blush at a raised voice in an office become, in a stadium or a square, capable of anything. The image is a seductive one — it flatters the reader, who is never part of the crowd in question — and it has shaped how police are trained, how stadiums are built and how newspapers report a disturbance. It is also, according to most researchers who now study the subject, largely wrong.

B. The evidence against it began to accumulate when investigators stopped relying on eyewitness accounts and started counting. Analysis of footage from emergencies — a fire in a nightclub, a crush at a station, an evacuation after an explosion — reveals a pattern that is almost the opposite of panic. Far from trampling one another, people tend to slow down, look for those they arrived with, and help strangers who have fallen. Deaths, when they occur, are seldom caused by a stampede in any meaningful sense; they are caused by too many bodies being funnelled through too small an exit, a failure of architecture rather than of character. Had the crowd behaved as the old theory predicts, the toll in such incidents would typically have been higher, not lower.

C. What, then, explains the disturbances that undeniably do happen? The most persuasive account holds that people in a crowd do not lose their identity so much as exchange it. A supporter who walks into a ground as an accountant walks out of it as a member of something larger, and the norms of that larger thing — not a hidden animal self — govern what he does next. Those norms can be generous or vicious, but they are norms all the same, and they are surprisingly sensitive to how the crowd is treated. Treat a peaceful gathering as a threat, and the gathering has a way of becoming one, since the bystanders who would otherwise have restrained the hotheads now share their grievance.

D. This has practical consequences that cut against instinct. Officers who patrol in pairs, talk to people and remove their helmets tend to see fewer arrests than those who form a line and wait. Festival organisers who post clear, honest information about delays report calmer queues than those who say nothing for fear of "alarming" anyone. The common thread is that the crowd is treated as a collection of adults capable of judgement, which, on the evidence, is exactly what it is.

E. None of this makes crowds safe, and no serious researcher claims it does. Density remains dangerous whatever the mood: above a certain number of bodies per square metre, physics takes over and intentions become irrelevant. The lesson is narrower and, in a way, more demanding. If the crowd is not a monster, then its worst moments cannot be blamed on some collective madness; they must be traced to decisions — about gates, about information, about tone — that somebody made. That is a less dramatic story than the mob of legend. It is also one in which the outcome can be changed.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) explains why the traditional view of crowds has remained so attractive?
questions.explanation: Section A calls the old image "seductive" and says it flatters the reader, who never imagines being part of the crowd described.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) argues that fatalities in emergencies are usually the result of design rather than behaviour?
questions.explanation: Section B says deaths are caused by bodies "funnelled through too small an exit, a failure of architecture rather than of character".

questions.q: Which section (A–E) describes how the way a crowd is handled can turn a calm gathering hostile?
questions.explanation: Section C: "Treat a peaceful gathering as a threat, and the gathering has a way of becoming one", because bystanders come to share the grievance.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) acknowledges a danger that no change of attitude can remove?
questions.explanation: Section E says density "remains dangerous whatever the mood": beyond a certain number of people per square metre, "physics takes over".

questions.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Eyewitness accounts of emergencies are generally more reliable than video footage
Crowds are far more dangerous than the public realises, and only better architecture can protect them
Crowds are not irrational mobs; their behaviour reflects shared norms and the way they are treated, so their worst moments can be prevented
Police forces have abandoned the old theory of crowds but festival organisers have not yet followed
questions.explanation: Every section builds the same case: the "mindless mob" is a myth, crowd behaviour is governed by norms and by treatment (C, D), and so its outcomes are the result of decisions that can be changed (E).

questions.q: What does the author's use of the phrase "some collective madness" in section E suggest about their attitude?
options: They believe it accurately describes a small minority of crowds
They think it is a term used only by police officers and journalists
They consider it the main cause of dangerous density in crowds
They regard it as a convenient explanation that lets the people who made decisions escape responsibility
questions.explanation: The sentence contrasts blaming "collective madness" with tracing events to "decisions that somebody made"; the word "some" is dismissive, and the point is that the mob story lets decision-makers off the hook. Nothing in the passage says the madness is real for any crowd.

questions.q: In section D, the phrase "cut against instinct" is closest in meaning to
options: contradict what people would naturally expect
reduce the need for training
are difficult to measure
are dangerous to carry out
questions.explanation: The consequences that follow — fewer arrests when officers remove helmets, calmer queues when delays are announced — are the opposite of what instinct would suggest; "cut against" means to go contrary to.

questions.q: According to the passage, most deaths in crowd emergencies are caused by people running over one another.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: False. Section B states that deaths "are seldom caused by a stampede in any meaningful sense" and blames exits that are too small for the number of people.

passages.title: Borrowed from the Air
passages.passage:
A bird in level flight is doing something that looks effortless and is anything but. Every second it is airborne, its weight pulls it towards the ground, and all that prevents this is the shape of its wing and the speed of the air across it. [1] Both features deflect the air downwards as it passes, and by Newton's third law, air pushed down means a wing pushed up. That upward push is lift, and when it equals the bird's weight, the bird neither rises nor falls.

Lift is never free. Deflecting air costs energy, and the cost shows up as drag, a backward force that grows sharply with speed. [2] Somewhere between the two lies a speed at which the total effort is lowest, and most birds, left to themselves, cruise close to it. A pigeon does not know the equation, but it descends from millions of generations in which those that flew inefficiently starved.

Flapping complicates the picture, because a flapping wing is a propeller and a wing at once. On the downstroke the wing is driven forwards and down, tilting the lift so that part of it points ahead and pulls the bird along. [3] Small birds make this cycle dozens of times a second; a heron completes it in a leisurely one.

The wingtips are where the most ingenious engineering is found. Because the pressure beneath a wing is higher than the pressure above it, air leaks around the tip from the underside to the top, curling into a vortex that trails behind the bird and wastes energy. [4] Aircraft designers, having reached the same conclusion eighty years later, now fit upturned "winglets" to airliners for exactly the same reason.

Then there is the question of size, which is why there are no sparrows the size of eagles. As an animal grows, its weight increases with the cube of its length while its wing area increases only with the square. [5] Beyond a certain point the sums no longer work, which is why the largest birds borrow their lift from rising air rather than manufacturing it with muscle: the condor and the albatross flap rarely and soar constantly. The very smallest, meanwhile, live in a world where the air feels thick and treacly, and the hummingbird's whirring hover is less like an eagle's flight than like a bee's.

A. Large soaring birds counter this by spreading their outermost feathers apart like fingers, breaking the single large vortex into several small ones that cost far less.
B. Unlike a bat's wing, feathers can be replaced one at a time when damaged.
C. A bird therefore faces a trade-off that any cyclist would recognise: go faster and the air resists you more; go slower and you must work harder to stay up at all.
D. A bird twice as long is therefore eight times as heavy but has only four times as much wing to hold it up.
E. Most migrating birds travel at night, when the air is cooler and predators fewer.
F. A wing is curved on top and flatter underneath, and it meets the oncoming air at a slight upward angle.
G. On the upstroke the wing is partly folded and twisted so that it slips through the air with as little resistance as possible.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [1]?
questions.explanation: The gap follows "the shape of its wing" and precedes "Both features deflect the air downwards"; F names the two features — the curved profile and the upward angle.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [2]?
questions.explanation: The next sentence says "Somewhere between the two lies a speed"; C supplies the two extremes (faster with more drag, slower with more effort) that the trade-off sits between.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [3]?
questions.explanation: The paragraph has just described the downstroke; G completes the cycle with the upstroke, and the following sentence refers to "this cycle".

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [4]?
questions.explanation: A begins "counter this", referring to the wasteful wingtip vortex just described, and it gives the birds' solution that aircraft designers later copied with winglets.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [5]?
questions.explanation: D turns the cube-and-square rule of the previous sentence into a concrete example (twice as long, eight times as heavy, four times the wing), leading into "the sums no longer work".

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: The reasons large birds are more efficient fliers than small ones
Why aircraft designers have always copied birds
The physical principles that allow birds to fly and the limits those principles impose
How different species of bird evolved different wing shapes
questions.explanation: The passage moves through lift, drag, flapping, wingtip vortices and the scaling problem of size: the physics of flight and its constraints. Aircraft and species differences are examples, not the theme.

questions.q: Why does the author mention that aircraft designers reached their conclusion "eighty years later"?
options: To show that winglets were invented before scientists understood birds
To suggest that evolution had arrived at a solution long before human engineering did
To explain why airliners are less efficient than large birds
To criticise engineers for ignoring biology
questions.explanation: The phrase follows a description of the "ingenious engineering" of feathered wingtips; saying humans reached "the same conclusion" much later quietly ranks nature ahead of the engineers. Nothing in the passage attacks engineers or compares aircraft efficiency.

questions.q: In the final paragraph, the word "treacly" is closest in meaning to
options: thick and sticky
warm and rising
fast-moving
thin and cold
questions.explanation: "Thick and treacly" describes how the air feels to a very small creature; treacle is a thick syrup, and the comparison with a bee reinforces the idea of moving through something resistant.

passages.title: Where the City's Dinner Goes
passages.passage:
A. Ask where a city's food waste comes from and most people picture the back door of a restaurant: sacks of peelings, unsold bread, plates scraped into a bin. Restaurants do waste food, but surveys in city after city tell a more uncomfortable story. In wealthy urban areas, more than half of the food that is thrown away is thrown away at home, and most of it was perfectly edible when it went into the bin. The problem is not a few careless businesses. It is millions of kitchens, each discarding a small amount for reasons that seem, at the time, entirely reasonable.

B. Those reasons are worth taking seriously, because a solution that ignores them will fail. Households buy more than they need because shops reward it, and because a fridge that looks full feels like security. They cook more than they eat because a small portion feels mean. They discard food that is still good because the date on the packet, which was printed to protect the manufacturer as much as the customer, told them to. And they do all this in cities that have made the bin the easiest option: a lid at the end of the kitchen, emptied by somebody else, with nothing to remind anyone what went in.

C. The obvious answer, urged by campaigners for decades, is to make people feel worse about it. Posters, school lessons and figures about the tonnage wasted each year have been tried in every large city, and the evidence on their effect is thin. Guilt, it turns out, is a poor instrument: it is felt strongly at the moment the poster is read and hardly at all at the moment the bin is opened. What moves the numbers is friction. When one European city introduced smaller general-waste bins alongside free food-waste caddies, the amount of edible food thrown away fell by nearly a third within a year, not because residents had been persuaded of anything but because the wrong bin had become slightly more trouble than the right one.

D. Further along the chain, the picture changes. Supermarkets discard produce not because it has spoiled but because it has stopped looking the way shoppers expect: a bent cucumber, an apple with a blemish, a loaf baked four hours ago. Here the waste is a business decision rather than a habit, and business decisions respond to prices. Where cities have taxed the disposal of edible food while making donation to charities cheap and legally safe, shops have discovered a sudden enthusiasm for giving it away. Nobody's conscience was awakened; the arithmetic simply changed.

E. What unites the successful schemes is that none of them relied on people becoming better than they are. They accepted that a tired parent at nine in the evening will do whatever is easiest, and that a store manager will do whatever is cheapest, and they arranged matters so that the easy and the cheap were also the right thing. It is a less inspiring approach than the posters, and it lacks their moral glow. It has the single advantage of working.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) challenges a popular assumption about who produces most of a city's food waste?
questions.explanation: Section A opens with the picture most people have (the restaurant back door) and then shows that more than half of the waste comes from homes.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) suggests that the design of the home itself makes wasting food easy?
questions.explanation: Section B ends by describing the bin as "the easiest option: a lid at the end of the kitchen, emptied by somebody else, with nothing to remind anyone what went in".

questions.q: Which section (A–E) explains why a widely used method of reducing waste has had little effect?
questions.explanation: Section C says posters and lessons have been tried everywhere with thin results because guilt is felt when the poster is read, not when the bin is opened.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) argues that shops throw food away for reasons that have nothing to do with its safety?
questions.explanation: Section D: supermarkets discard produce "not because it has spoiled but because it has stopped looking the way shoppers expect".

questions.q: Which of the following best summarises the writer's argument?
options: Waste falls when cities make the right choice the easiest or cheapest one, rather than when they appeal to conscience
European cities have solved the food-waste problem by taxing supermarkets
Food waste will only fall when citizens are properly educated about its cost to the planet
Restaurants and supermarkets, not households, are the real source of urban food waste
questions.explanation: Sections C, D and E all make the same point: guilt fails, while changes to convenience (bins) and cost (taxes, cheap donation) succeed because they do not require people to become better than they are.

questions.q: What does the writer imply about the "moral glow" of the poster campaigns in section E?
options: It is a quality that supermarkets lack but households possess
It is what makes such campaigns appealing to their supporters, even though it is not what reduces waste
It is the main reason the campaigns have succeeded in some cities
It has been deliberately copied by the designers of the bin schemes
questions.explanation: The writer concedes the practical schemes are "less inspiring" and lack the posters' glow, then adds that they have "the single advantage of working" — implying the glow is attractive to people but beside the point. The passage never says the posters succeeded anywhere.

questions.q: In section C, the word "friction" is used to mean
options: a strong emotional reaction
disagreement between neighbours
a small practical obstacle that makes an action less convenient
heat produced when surfaces rub together
questions.explanation: The example that follows explains it: waste fell because "the wrong bin had become slightly more trouble than the right one" — a minor inconvenience, not an argument or an emotion.

questions.q: The European city described in section C charged its residents for the food-waste caddies it introduced.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: False. The passage says the city introduced smaller general-waste bins "alongside free food-waste caddies".

passages.title: In Defence of the Empty Hour
passages.passage:
Boredom has a poor reputation among the emotions. Fear warns us, anger protects us, grief honours what we have lost; boredom, by contrast, seems to do nothing but complain. [1] For most of history it was barely discussed, and when it was, it was as a moral failing — the sin of the monk who could not bring himself to pray. Only in the last two centuries has it been treated as something that might deserve an explanation rather than a rebuke.

The philosophers who took it seriously reached an unsettling conclusion. Boredom, they suggested, is not the absence of stimulation but the presence of a question that stimulation normally hides. [2] The child who groans "there's nothing to do" is wrong about the facts — there is a great deal to do — and right about something deeper: none of it, at that moment, seems to matter. Seen this way, boredom is less like hunger than like doubt.

If that is so, then the modern cure may be worse than the disease. We now carry in our pockets a device whose entire purpose is to ensure that the question never arises. [3] Never before has it been so easy to avoid being bored, and rarely has so much been said about how bored everyone is. The two facts are not in tension. An appetite fed constantly with sweets does not go away; it simply loses the ability to recognise a meal.

There is a further cost, and it is a creative one. Studies that give people a dull task before a test of imagination have found, fairly consistently, that the dull task helps. [4] Writers and mathematicians have long reported the same thing in plainer language: the idea arrives in the shower, on the walk, in the waiting room — anywhere the mind has been left unattended for a while.

None of this is a recommendation to seek boredom out, any more than to seek out doubt. [5] The claim is more modest. Boredom is a signal, and like any signal it can be silenced or heeded. Silence it, and it returns in a form harder to name — as restlessness, as a vague dissatisfaction with a life that by every visible measure is full. Heed it, and it asks a question that is worth an honest answer: not "what can I do?" but "what is worth doing?" The empty hour is not a problem to be solved. It is, on occasion, the only room in the house where that question can be heard.

A. The moment a queue forms or a conversation pauses, a screen fills the gap before the gap can be noticed.
B. Both are uncomfortable, and both, endured for too long, curdle into something closer to despair.
C. This is why many thinkers have argued that happiness is impossible without leisure.
D. It is the feeling of a mind that wants to be occupied and cannot find anything worth occupying it.
E. When nothing demands our attention, we are left alone with the matter of what, if anything, is worth attending to.
F. The most bored people, surveys suggest, are those with the most demanding jobs.
G. Deprived of anything interesting outside itself, the mind begins to generate interest from within, wandering, combining, rehearsing possibilities.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [1]?
questions.explanation: The paragraph has just said boredom "seems to do nothing but complain"; D defines what that complaint is, and the next sentence ("For most of history it was barely discussed") refers back to the feeling.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [2]?
questions.explanation: The previous sentence says stimulation hides "a question"; E states the question (what is worth attending to), and the child's complaint that follows illustrates it.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [3]?
questions.explanation: A describes the pocket "device" in action — a screen filling every pause — and leads into "Never before has it been so easy to avoid being bored".

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [4]?
questions.explanation: G explains why the dull task helps: the mind starts producing its own interest. The next sentence says writers have "reported the same thing", which is this wandering of the unattended mind.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [5]?
questions.explanation: The previous sentence pairs boredom with doubt; B's "Both are uncomfortable" picks up that pair, and "The claim is more modest" then follows naturally.

questions.q: Which statement best captures the writer's central claim?
options: Boredom is a signal worth attending to, because it raises a question that constant distraction prevents us from hearing
People should deliberately make themselves bored in order to become more creative
Philosophers have always regarded boredom as the most important of the emotions
Boredom is a moral weakness that modern technology has finally cured
questions.explanation: The passage reframes boredom as "the presence of a question", warns that phones silence it, and concludes that it should be "heeded". The final paragraph explicitly denies that we should seek boredom out.

questions.q: What does the writer mean by saying that the two facts "are not in tension"?
options: Surveys about boredom are unreliable because people exaggerate
People who complain of boredom are usually the ones without phones
Being bored and avoiding boredom are two ways of describing the same experience
Constant distraction is the very reason boredom is now so widely complained of, not evidence against the argument
questions.explanation: The sweets analogy that follows makes the link: an appetite fed constantly with distraction "loses the ability to recognise a meal", so the ease of avoiding boredom and the volume of complaint about it are cause and effect rather than a contradiction.

questions.q: In piece B, the phrase "curdle into" is closest in meaning to
options: become stronger and healthier
be mixed together with
gradually turn into something worse
suddenly disappear
questions.explanation: Milk curdles when it goes off; the metaphor describes an uncomfortable state deteriorating, "endured for too long", into despair.
